Alternatively, you may apply to serve as an Associate Editor-in-Chief for one of the subtopics listed below. To express your interest, please send us an email indicating whether you would like to serve as the Editor-in-Chief for the entire topic or as an Associate Editor-in-Chief for a specific subtopic. Be sure to attach your CV and/or a biographical sketch to your application. The term pre-medical (commonly abbreviated as pre-med) refers to the academic and extracurricular track pursued by undergraduate students in the United States who are preparing to apply to medical school. This track encompasses a variety of activities designed to prepare students for medical school, including pre-med coursework, volunteer work, clinical experience, research, and the medical school application process. Pre-Med Timeline During their first year of college, pre-med students typically structure their coursework to include the required classes for medical school. After completing a semester, many students begin engaging in extracurricular activities that demonstrate their commitment to the field of medicine. By their junior year, students usually register for and take the Medical College Admission Test (MCAT), a standardized exam required by medical schools to evaluate qualified candidates. After taking the MCAT, students apply to medical schools through the American Medical College Application Service (AMCAS) or through individual application systems for schools that do not use AMCAS. The application process involves a comprehensive review of the applicant's coursework, extracurricular activities, work experience, and a personal statement. Applicants can expect to receive responses from medical schools within several weeks. At this stage, they may be asked to complete secondary applications, which are specific to each school and often include essay questions. Applicants who meet the qualifications may then be invited to interview at certain schools. Receiving an interview invitation is considered a significant milestone, reflecting the effort and dedication invested in building a strong application. Once the interview process is completed, the application is considered complete, and applicants await final decisions from the schools. Coursework The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) has established a set of standard required courses that all pre-med students must complete. However, individual medical schools may impose additional requirements. Pre-med coursework is offered at many colleges and universities in the United States and is considered a track that follows a specific curriculum. Most pre-med students major in natural sciences, such as biology, chemistry, or physics, although this is not a strict requirement. Approximately 25% of medical school matriculants major in fields outside the natural and physical sciences, such as anthropology, philosophy, or other humanities disciplines. The typical courses required for pre-med students include: General Chemistry I & II (with laboratory components) General Biology I & II (with laboratory components; some schools allow zoology as a substitute for the second semester) Organic Chemistry I & II (with laboratory components; some schools allow biochemistry as a substitute for the second semester) General Physics I & II (with laboratory components) One or two semesters of mathematics, usually Calculus I and either Calculus II or a statistics course English and writing courses In addition to these core requirements, pre-med students may be advised or required to take upper-level biology and chemistry electives, such as cellular biology, physical chemistry, biochemistry, genetics, and others. Specific requirements for these courses vary by institution. Some medical schools also have requirements for non-science courses. For example, certain schools may require a specific number of general humanities credits, while others may mandate coursework in English, psychology, or other disciplines. Pre-Med in Other Countries In Australia, several universities offer threeor four-year Bachelor of Medical Science or Biomedical Science degrees. These programs are similar in content and purpose to pre-med courses in the United States, as the majority of graduates aim to gain entry into graduate medical schools.
